markup: One typo cost a Tokyo bank {¥40|forty} {billion.|billion yen.}
And it sold shares... that didn't even exist.
December {8th,|eighth,} {2005.|two thousand five.}
A small company called J-Com starts trading on the Tokyo Stock Exchange.
It has only about {14,500|fourteen thousand five hundred} shares.
At Mizuho Securities, a trader gets a simple job:
sell one share, for {¥610,000.|six hundred and ten thousand yen.}
He types... {610,000|six hundred and ten thousand} shares... for {¥1.|one yen.}
Easy mistake.
That's {41|forty-one} times more shares than the whole company has.
But how do you sell something that doesn't exist?
"Cancel it!"
They press cancel.
Nothing.
Again.
Nothing.
The price crashes to the floor.
And all over Japan, buyers grab the cheap shares.
One {27-year-old|twenty-seven-year-old} with an online account makes over {¥2|two} {billion.|billion yen.}
You see, a stock exchange is like a giant notice board.
You pin up "selling", and it doesn't stop to check if you really have it.
And the cancel button?
The exchange's own system had a bug.
Mizuho bought most shares back.
But over {96,000|ninety-six thousand} of them never existed, so it paid cash instead.
The bill: about {¥40|forty} {billion.|billion yen.}
Years later, a court ruled the exchange had to pay part of it.
The typo took one second.
The fight over it took eight years.
